questions.q: Why does this lesson say a security architecture review process is needed even for a skilled, well-intentioned architect?
options: Because Salesforce legally requires a review board for every org
Because architects are not trusted to configure Health Check correctly
Because a single person deep inside their own design reliably misses things a second reviewer, who wasn't anchored on the same assumptions, catches on a fresh read
Because review boards replace the need for threat modeling
questions.explain: The review process exists because of a structural blind spot, not a trust issue -- someone deep inside their own design's tradeoffs reliably misses things that a reviewer without that same anchoring catches, the same reason code review exists for code.

questions.q: What does Salesforce's Health Check score actually measure?
options: How well custom Apex code enforces CRUD and field-level security
Whether record-sharing rules are configured according to least privilege
How many integrations are connected to the org
How closely an org's actual security settings (like password policy and session settings) match Salesforce's recommended baseline or a custom baseline, weighted by risk tier
questions.explain: Health Check scores org-wide settings like password policy and session configuration against a recommended (or custom) baseline, weighted so high-risk settings count more -- it does not evaluate record-level sharing design, custom code, or integration scoping.

questions.q: In the Lab scenario, why wouldn't the org's Health Check score alone have caught the problem with the newly approved integration (Connected App scoped to `full`, integration user granted "View All Data")?
options: Because Health Check measures org-wide settings like password policy and session configuration, not Connected App OAuth scopes or an individual integration user's object permissions
Because Health Check would have automatically blocked the integration from being created
Because Health Check only applies to Sandbox orgs, not Production
Because the integration issue is unrelated to any security concern covered in this course
questions.explain: Health Check's scope is org-wide settings such as password and session policy -- it has no visibility into a specific Connected App's OAuth scope or a specific integration user's object-level permissions, which is exactly why the lesson stresses Health Check is one input, not a replacement for the full review checklist.

questions.q: What is a "custom baseline" in the context of Health Check?
options: A permanent downgrade of the Health Check score to account for known weaknesses
An alternative, organization-specific set of required settings that Health Check can score against instead of Salesforce's generic default recommendation
A feature that disables Health Check scoring entirely
A record of every Apex class that has ever been deployed to the org
questions.explain: A custom baseline lets an organization with specific regulatory requirements score its settings against its own required configuration rather than Salesforce's generic recommended baseline.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the point of offering a "lightweight" review option for smaller changes, instead of requiring the full review board every time?
options: So that small changes can skip security review entirely
So that only large changes are ever reviewed, since small changes are never risky
So that every change gets some deliberate check proportional to its risk, rather than nothing being checked because a change seemed too small for the full heavyweight process
Because Salesforce does not allow full review boards for changes smaller than a certain size
questions.explain: The lightweight option -- a self-answered checklist plus a single peer sign-off -- exists so small changes still get a proportional, deliberate check instead of none at all, while reserving the full review board for changes that actually warrant it.
